quiz_item.question: When planning a major family purchase under Requirement 1, why should you compare total cost of ownership and financing options across multiple retailers rather than looking only at the monthly payment?
options: A. Because a lower monthly payment always guarantees a lower total purchase price and zero interest charges.
B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.
C. Because retail stores are legally required to match the lowest monthly payment offered by any online auction site.
D. Because comparison shopping only applies to consumable groceries and does not affect durable goods or warranties.
choices: A. Because a lower monthly payment always guarantees a lower total purchase price and zero interest charges.
B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.
C. Because retail stores are legally required to match the lowest monthly payment offered by any online auction site.
D. Because comparison shopping only applies to consumable groceries and does not affect durable goods or warranties.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Evaluating needs versus wants, comparison shopping for quality and price, and calculating interest, warranties, and operating expenses reveals the true total cost of a major purchase.

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Prepare a budget reflecting your expected income (allowance, gifts, wages), expenses, and savings for a period of 13 consecutive weeks. (b) Compare expected income with expected expenses. (1) If expenses exceed budget income, determine steps to balance your budget. (2) If income exceeds budget expenses, state how you would use the excess money (new goal, savings). (c) Track and record your actual income, expenses, and savings for 13 consecutive weeks (the same 13-week period for which you budgeted). (You may use the forms provided in the Personal Management merit badge pamphlet, devise your own, or use a computer-generated version.) When complete, present the records showing the results to your counselor. (d) Compare your budget with your actual income and expenses to understand when your budget worked and when it did not work. With your counselor, discuss what you might do differently the next time.

pamphlet_excerpts: Personal Management Core Field Standard: By the time you reach your late teens, you probably will have received numerous offers from credit card companies to apply for their cards (p. 39).
Personal Management Core Field Standard Principle 2: Just remember that you are personally responsible and legally obligated to pay back all amounts charged to your card (p. 39).
Personal Management Core Field Standard Principle 3: A credit card is a form of loan, just as if you had borrowed cash from a financial institution (p. 39).
Personal Management Core Field Standard Principle 4: It can be a convenient substitute for carrying checks or a large amount of cash and especially useful in emergencies (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): In fact, credit cards do represent real money; using them unwisely can lead to financial difficulties (p. 39).

Step 2 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): A credit card, issued by a financial institution or credit card company, can be used to pay for any product or service as long as the seller accepts (p. 39).
Step 3 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): Not all sellers accept credit cards or a particular type of credit card, however (p. 39).
Step 4 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): In addition, credit cards have a charge limit, which means you can charge only up to the amount the credit card issuerallows (p. 39).

requirements.req_text: Demonstrate to your counselor your understanding of time management by doing the following: (a) Write a to-do list of tasks or activities, such as homework assignments, chores, and personal projects, that must be done in the coming week. List these in order of importance to you. (b) Make a seven-day calendar or schedule. Put in your set activities, such as school classes, sports practices or games, jobs or chores, and/or Scout or place of worship or club meetings, then plan when you will do all the tasks from your to-do list between your set activities. (c) Follow the one-week schedule you planned. Keep a daily diary or journal during each of the seven days of this week's activities, writing down when you completed each of the tasks on your to-do list compared to when you scheduled them. (d) With your counselor, review your to-do list, one-week schedule, and diary/journal to understand when your schedule worked and when it did not work. Discuss what you might do differently the next time.
